record.original_question: (stronger version of Dejean’s conjecture): – For every k ≥ 5, an infinite (k/k − 1)+ -free word over k letters exists with letter frequency 1/k + 1. – For every k ≥ 6, an infinite (k/k−1)+ -free word over k-letter exists with letter frequency 1/k − 1.

evidence.quote: (stronger version of Dejean’s conjecture): – For every k ≥ 5, an infinite (k/k − 1)+ -free word over k letters exists with letter frequency 1/k + 1. – For every k ≥ 6, an infinite (k/k−1)+ -free word over k-letter exists with letter frequency 1/k − 1.
The conjecture has been completely solved by Michaël Rao (private communication at WORDS 2015).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For an integer k ≥ 2 and a real number α > 1, an infinite word w over a k-letter alphabet is called α⁺-free if it contains no factor of the form u^e with rational exponent e > α (where u^e denotes a prefix of length ⌈e·|u|⌉ of the infinite repetition u·u·u·…). The repetition threshold for k letters is known to equal k/(k−1) for k ≥ 5 (Dejean's theorem). For an infinite word w over a k-letter alphabet, the frequency of a letter a is the limit (when it exists) of the ratio (number of occurrences of a in the prefix of length n)/n, as n → ∞.

Prove or disprove the following two statements:

(a) For every integer k ≥ 5, there exists an infinite (k/(k−1))⁺-free word over a k-letter alphabet in which some letter has frequency exactly 1/(k+1).

(b) For every integer k ≥ 6, there exists an infinite (k/(k−1))⁺-free word over a k-letter alphabet in which some letter has frequency exactly 1/(k−1).
artifact.status_search_result: The two statements form a stronger frequency-version of Dejean's conjecture. Initial cases (k=5 with frequency 1/6, k=6 with frequency 1/5) were established by Chalopin and Ochem (2008). The full conjecture was reported as completely solved by Michaël Rao (announced at WORDS 2015), in the same line of work in which Rao settled the remaining cases of Dejean's conjecture.
